Quit the editor the way that editor quits. The pane comes back by itself.
In Vim or Neovim, press Esc, then type :q and Enter. If it reports unsaved changes, type :q! and Enter instead.
:q! is safe here. The file is a copy, and herdr deletes it as soon as the editor exits. Discarding the changes loses nothing.
The pane you started from kept running the whole time. Nothing was waiting on you, and focus returns to that pane on its own.
The editor is whatever EDITOR names, so another setup may quit some other way. The section on which editor runs covers that.

prefix+e copies the focused pane's stored history into a temp file, then opens $EDITOR on that file in a second pane. The key name is keys.edit_scrollback, listed with its default in herdr's config reference.
herdr takes the copy once, at the moment of the keypress, and never updates it. While the editor is open the pane goes on printing into its own history, and the file stays as written.
Whatever you save in the editor stays in the copy. The pane keeps the history it had.

Reading a long pane history in an editor you already know. Copy mode offers literal search with / and ?, described in herdr's keyboard reference. An editor adds regular expressions, folding, marks, and split windows over the same text.

For a history longer than that, the keypress is the way to see all of it at once.
Working from the keyboard alone. The key acts on the focused pane, so there is no pane id to look up and no shell to run a command in.
Up to 1000 rows, both routes call the same function and return the same bytes (src/app/api_helpers.rs:120-129). The gain is the editor, so a script is better served by the command.

Derive the session in the shell prompt from $HERDR_SOCKET_PATH, which every pane gets: the default session is ~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock, a named one is ~/.config/herdr/sessions/<name>/herdr.sock. $HERDR_SESSION is only inherited from the server process — present for named sessions, unset on the default — while HERDR_ENV, HERDR_SOCKET_PATH, HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID, HERDR_TAB_ID, and HERDR_PANE_ID are injected deliberately.
Set the outer terminal title yourself before launching, from a wrapper that emits OSC 2 alongside herdr session attach <name>. Nothing in 0.8.0 will overwrite it.

With the flag false the third step is skipped and a pane nobody named stays blank. Turning it on costs nothing where a name already exists, since the first two steps still win.
What the border title shows, in order
Splits only. herdr draws pane borders only when a tab holds more than one pane, so a lone pane carries no label however much the agent reports.
Needs ui.pane_borders = true (the default). Under ui.pane_outer_borders = false the outer edges drop their borders, so the top row of panes loses the border the title is drawn on.
The title sits at the left end of the top border as name , truncated with … to the pane width minus four — narrow panes show a stub, and a pane four columns wide or less shows nothing.
Focused panes render it bold in the accent color, unfocused panes in the dim border color.

herdr agent rename <target> <name> does not change the border. It sets the agent's unique name, which is how the CLI and sidebar address that agent; the border reads the display-agent metadata field instead. herdr pane rename is the one that renames a border.

A screen-detected label vanishes the moment the agent process exits, rather than leaving a stale claude sitting over a plain shell. Hook-reported agents keep their label while the hook authority is live.
